title: Quip Network Lets Anyone Set A Price For Quantum Computing Time
excerpt: Quip Network lets anyone set a price for quantum computing time, offering a decentralized marketplace.
content:
A 23-stop route for a delivery truck would take a conventional computer approximately 18,000 years to optimize, illustrating the scale of problems quantum computing aims to solve. Postquant Labs is now offering a new approach with Quip Network, a decentralized marketplace where anyone can post optimization jobs and set a reward for the solution, the company says. Unlike D-Wave’s Leap service, which does not have a public per-use rate, Quip Network allows users to define payment for successful results delivered by a network of miners using CPUs, GPUs and quantum annealers.

D-Wave and Quip Network: System Architecture & Access

Quip Network currently operates a testnet, a preliminary version of the platform open to developers, with a full transition to mainnet planned following an external audit of its chain code. D-Wave’s Advantage2 quantum processing unit (QPU) boasts over 4,400 qubits and more than 40,000 couplers, with an average of 20 couplers per qubit, while Quip Network’s architecture is designed to be hardware agnostic. This means Quip Network can use a diverse range of computational resources, including central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), and quantum annealers.

The platform currently supports D-Wave systems and plans to integrate additional hardware types in the future. Quip Network employs a reward-based system where users define the payment for solving a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, paid to the miners who successfully complete the task.

This contrasts with D-Wave’s contract pricing model, which does not disclose a public per-use rate, according to the company. Quip Network’s XQuad toolchain converts QUBOs into Ising models, encoding coefficients as thousandths to ensure consistent energy calculations across different hardware types. While D-Wave returns samples and their associated energies, Quip Network’s chain recomputes the energy of every submitted answer and enforces user-defined quality thresholds.

At the Quantum.Tech World event, a D-Wave Advantage QPU competed against simulated annealing on 1,930 portfolio optimization problems submitted by attendees, with each problem run as a job on the Quip Network, the firm reports. The same QUBO, a mathematical formulation of optimization problems, can be processed on both D-Wave and Quip Network, though the methods of encoding and execution differ.

D-Wave uses its SDK to store QUBOs as binary quadratic models, while Quip Network’s XQuad converts them into Ising models. The platform guides users through posting a QUBO to the Aglais testnet, providing access to free AGLS tokens to cover initial computational costs.
